newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk troops clash with rebels in northern Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turk troops clash with rebels in northern Iraq.

text.p: Turkish troops clashed with Kurdish guerrillas in northern Iraq on Monday as Turkey's cross-border incursion drew increasing fire from neighbouring countries, rebel sources said.

Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) guerrillas fought with Turkish soldiers and an allied Iraqi Kurdish militia in the Zap, Metina and Haftanin valleys of northern Iraq, the Germany-based DEM news agency, which is close to the rebels, said in a statement.
It said the Turkish forces had sustained "heavy casualties".
Turkish military officials said on Sunday they had consolidated their hold on the region, bringing the strategic Zap Valley under control after five days of fierce fighting.
Anatolian news agency quoted General Altay Tokat as saying 1,750 rebels had been killed or wounded in the operation so far. Western diplomats say the figures are inflated.

More than 10,000 Turkish troops, allied with the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), poured into northern Iraq last Wednesday in pursuit of PKK rebels who use the region as a base to launch raids into southeast Turkey.
Iraq's ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra on Monday urged the United Nations to take action to force Turkish troops to leave the area.

"Denunciation alone will not be enough to force Turkey to withdraw its invasion troops from Iraqi territories. What is needed is a stronger attitude, more determined, more decisive from the United Nations which will force Turkey to reconsider its stand and pull out its troops," Thawra said in a commentary.
The fighting is taking place in a Western-protected Kurdish enclave that has been out of Baghdad's control since the end of the 1991 Gulf War.
Iran has protested to Turkey over its cross-border offensive and urged it to withdraw immediately.

The official Iranian news agency IRNA said Turkey's charge d'affaires in Tehran was summoned to the foreign ministry on Sunday night and informed of "Iran's protest and Tehran's concern over the continued military presence of Turkey in northern Iraq".
Turkish foreign ministry spokesman Omer Akbel said Ankara was disappointed at Tehran's lack of cooperation in the fight against the PKK.

"We would have wished that Iran had shown concern for the PKK activities in the region and thus would have cooperated more fully with Turkey in combatting the terrorism of the PKK," he told a news briefing.

Turkish military authorities opened the region to selected Turkish journalists and film crews at the weekend, giving them a tour of the Zap Valley. Otherwise a ban on correspondents, imposed at the start of the operation, remained in force.
Television pictures showed two bodies, said to be those of PKK rebels, and large amounts of ammunition the army said it had captured from the guerrillas.
Turkey mounted a six-week, 35,000-man operation into the Kurdish-held northern Iraqi regions two years ago but failed to achieve its stated aim of clearing the area of PKK.
Turkish officials have said Iran, Syria and Iraq were building up military forces on the borders of the Iraqi Kurdish region to help rebels escape.
